content.text: Share fairly: how many apples will each child get?
Identify one half and one quarter of a shape split into two or four equal parts.
Find one half of an even number of objects up to 20 by sharing them into two equal groups.
Find one quarter of 4, 8, 12, 16 or 20 objects by sharing them into four equal groups.
Equal parts are the same size.

elements.name: Diagram
elements.alt: Two matching rectangles: one has one of two equal parts shaded; the other has one of four equal parts shaded.

slides.notes:
Running
Spend about 4 minutes. Read the definitions together. Ask pupils to point to one half and one quarter in the diagrams, then explain what makes the parts equal.

Misconceptions
Pupils may think any two parts make halves, even if the parts are different sizes. Reinforce that equal parts must be the same size. A quarter is one of four equal parts, not one of four unequal parts.

Background
The words half and quarter describe equal shares: half means one of two equal parts, and quarter means one of four. The parts do not have to be the same shape, but they must have equal size.

content.text: Which shaded part shows one quarter?
One of 2 equal parts is shaded.
One of 4 equal parts is shaded.
One of 4 unequal parts is shaded.

slides.notes:
Running
Spend about 4 minutes. Pupils choose independently, then compare with a partner and explain why the parts must be equal.

Answers
B: One of 4 equal parts is shaded.

Misconceptions
Choosing the first option shows pupils may think a shaded part is a quarter whenever there are two parts; that is a half. Choosing the third shows they may ignore whether the parts are equal. A quarter is one of four equal parts.

content.text: Count one group: half of 8 is 4.

elements.name: Diagram
elements.alt: Eight counters shared into two equal groups of four.

slides.notes:
Running
Spend about 5 minutes. Model sharing the counters one at a time between two groups. Count one group together and check that both groups have 4.

Misconceptions
Pupils may count both groups and answer 8, rather than counting one group. Emphasise that half of 8 is the number in one of the two equal groups: 4.

Background
Sharing into two equal groups is a practical way to find half. Each counter belongs to one group, so the two group totals are equal and together make the starting amount.

elements.name: Diagram
elements.alt: Ten counters shared equally between two rings. Find the number in one ring.

content.text: Find one half of 10. Count one group.

slides.notes:
Running
Spend about 4 minutes. Pupils work alone with counters or a drawing, share 10 into two equal groups and write how many are in one group. Check answers together.

Answers
5

Misconceptions
Pupils may answer 10 by counting all the counters, or make unequal groups and still call one group half. Share one counter at a time between two groups; each group has 5.

content.text: Count one group: a quarter of 12 is 3.

elements.name: Diagram
elements.alt: Twelve counters shared into four equal groups of three.

slides.notes:
Running
Spend about 5 minutes. Model sharing 12 counters one at a time into four groups. Count one group together and check that the four groups total 12.

Misconceptions
Pupils may count all 12 counters, or share them into two groups and call one group a quarter. A quarter needs four equal groups; one group has 3.

Background
Finding a quarter of a set means dividing the whole set into four equal groups and taking the amount in one group. This is also one way to calculate 12 ÷ 4.

elements.name: Diagram
elements.alt: Sixteen counters shared equally between four rings. Find the number in one ring.

content.text: Find one quarter of 16. Count one group.

slides.notes:
Running
Spend about 4 minutes. Pupils work alone or in pairs with counters or drawings. They make four equal groups, count one group and record the answer.

Answers
4

Misconceptions
Pupils may make two groups, or count all 16 instead of one of four equal groups. Share 16 into four equal groups; there are 4 in each group.

content.text: How do you find one quarter of 8 counters?

slides.notes:
Running
Spend about 4 minutes. Pupils select a method independently, then justify their choice to a partner. Invite the class to use the method to find a quarter of 8.

Answers
B: Make 4 equal groups; count one.

Misconceptions
Choosing the first option shows pupils are finding a half, not a quarter. Choosing the third shows they know to make four groups but count the whole amount rather than one group. One quarter of 8 is one of four equal groups.

elements.name: Diagram
elements.alt: A is a square with one of two equal triangles shaded. B is a rectangle with one of four equal horizontal strips shaded.

content.text: Name the shaded fraction in A and B. Explain how you know.

slides.notes:
Running
Spend about 5 minutes. Pupils write the name of each shaded fraction and explain their reasoning to a partner. Ask a few pupils to say how the number of equal parts helped them decide.

Answers
A is one half; B is one quarter.

Misconceptions
Pupils may name a fraction by the shape or direction of the dividing line rather than by the number of equal parts and the number shaded. Check that the parts are equal: one of two is a half, and one of four is a quarter.

Background
A diagonal line can split a square into two equal triangles. A rectangle split into four equal horizontal strips has four equal parts. The fraction depends on how many equal parts there are and how many are shaded.

content.text: Draw equal groups. Write each answer.

slides.notes:
Running
Spend about 8 minutes. Pupils draw counters and circle two equal groups for the half, then four equal groups for each quarter. They write the number in one group as each answer. Review one example together.

Answers
1. 9
2. 2
3. 5

Misconceptions
Pupils may count the whole set instead of one group, or make the wrong number of groups. For half, share into two equal groups; for a quarter, share into four equal groups, then count one group.

Background
The answers can be checked by combining the equal groups: two groups of 9 make 18; four groups of 2 make 8; and four groups of 5 make 20.

content.text: Half of 14 birds fly away. How many stay?
Share 12 buns fairly on 4 plates. How many per plate?
Stretch: find half and a quarter of 16. Which is more?
Draw your sharing. Explain your answers.

slides.notes:
Running
Spend about 10 minutes. Pupils draw or use counters to solve the first two problems, then complete the stretch if ready. Ask them to explain how their equal groups show each answer.

Answers
1. 7 birds stay.
2. 3 buns per plate.
3. Half of 16 is 8; a quarter of 16 is 4. Half is more.

Misconceptions
For the birds, pupils may give 7 as the number that fly away rather than the number that stay; half of 14 fly away, so the other half, 7, stay. For the buns, sharing into two groups finds a half, not a quarter; four plates need four equal groups of 3. In the stretch, pupils may think the quarter is larger because the number 4 is mentioned; compare the amounts, 8 and 4.

Background
These problems apply equal sharing to everyday contexts. In the bird question, the remaining birds are the other equal half. In the bun question, fair sharing means every plate gets the same number.
